newsitem.title: USA: Dlr rebounds from sell-off to close higher in U.S..
newsitem.headline: Dlr rebounds from sell-off to close higher in U.S..

text.p: The dollar bounced back from a sell-off to finish firmer, buttressed by a well-bid U.S. Treasury bond sale and comments from New York Federal Reserve Bank President William McDonough, currency experts said.
The $10 billion U.S. Treasury 30-year bond sale garnered solid demand on Thursday, with an average yield of 6.618 percent compared to an expected average yield of 6.63 percent.
"The bond market made a nice recovery after the 30-year auction," said Lizbeth Goldberg, an assistant vice president at Hypobank. "The bonds are coming up (and) the dollar's coming up slightly."
The dollar had tumbled to intraday lows of 111.27 yen and 1.5040 marks in New York before erasing its losses.
The U.S. unit finished at 112.10/15 yen and 1.5124/29 marks, up from 111.55/65 yen and 1.5069/72 marks at the open.
Speaking to the Spanish Institute here, New York Fed President McDonough said European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) will most likely take off as planned in 1999.
McDonough cited the political will among Eurpean leaders to make EMU work as a key reason behind his thinking.
"That helped the dollar," said Elliott Dix, an assitant vice president at Signet Bank.
Dix noted the mark would loose some strength, while the Italian and French currencies would tend to gain because investors can hold those currencies for the yields.
Earlier in the session, the dollar had tumbled against the yen after comments by a senior Japanese offical and the head of a U.S. manufacturers group.

Nikkei Financial Daily newspaper on Thursday had quoted Eisuke Sakakibara as saying the dollar correction from last year's sharp slide against the yen was about finished and the Ministry of Finance was not trying to weaken the yen further.
When questioned by reporters later, Sakakibara, director-general of the International Finance Bureau, stood by his remarks.
Sakakibara also said the financial markets' view of the Japanese economy was too pessimistic and the economy was stronger than the markets expected.

This assessment was echoed by the Director-General of Japan's Economic Planning Agency, Taro Aso, who said the economic recovery is still moderate but emphasized conditions have improved from two or three months ago.

"The Japanese government feels that the yen does not need to weaken any further and that the economy is a little stronger than it's been given credit for," said David Durrant, a senior currency strategist at I.D.E.A. Inc.
Durrant predicted the dollar's decline against the yen is not finished.
Remarks by Jerry Jasinowski, president of the National Association of Manufacturers, added to the dollars woes on Thursday, some experts said.
Jasinowski predicted the White House will de-emphasize the value of a strong dollar as the U.S. economy slows.
Such a change would contrast with the policy adopted by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, who has repeatedly called for a strong dollar.
Dix doubted Rubin would endorse a weak dollar. "I think he would recognize that the dollar strength is very important to the U.S. economy drawing investment from overseas," he added.

The dollar ended at 1.2738/48 Swiss francs, up from 1.2640/45 at the open. Sterling rose to $1.6475/85 from $1.6430/40. The dollar slid to Canadian $1.3290/95 from C$1.3324/29. The Australian dollar closed at $0.7835/40.
-- Donna Sells 212 859-1668
